Lecture 3 Range, Quartiles and Box Plots; Sets, Sample Spaces and the Probability Axioms

The rest of the measures of spread (range, quartiles, interquartile range), the five-number summary, the 1.5 × IQR outlier rule and how to draw a box plot. Then the start of probability: set operations, experiments, sample spaces, events and the three probability axioms.

1Other measures of variability: the range and the interquartile range

Other measures of variability or spread:

Definition ① The range

This is the length of the shortest interval that contains all the data values.

Example example

a)  

b)  

✎ Explanation (added)

Range largest value smallest value. The two data sets were chosen to have the same smallest and largest values and therefore the same range, even though a) has its values pushed out to the two ends and b) has them gathered in the middle. That is exactly the weakness he points out next.

Textbook · Devore — the range and why it is not enough by itself: §1.4, p. 36, with Figure 1.18.

By itself, the range is not a very good measure of spread.

It tells us nothing about how the data values are spread out on the interval.

Definition

A slightly [better] measure is the interquartile range. (IQR)

This tells us about the length of the interval containing the middle half of the data. (When using samples, the book calls this the fourth spread).

On the board the sentence reads “A slightly measure is the interquartile range”; the word “better” is missing and is supplied here in brackets.

✎ Explanation (added)

The range only looks at two values, the two most extreme ones, so a single unusual value changes it completely. The IQR ignores the lowest quarter and the highest quarter of the data and measures how wide the middle 50% is, so extreme values cannot move it. “Fourth spread” is Devore’s name for the same idea (Devore §1.4), written .

Textbook · Devore — fourths and the fourth spread: Definition in §1.4, p. 40.

2Finding the quartiles

To find the IQR, we need to find the first and third quartiles which we will denote by and   (book: upper and lower fourths).

Our goal is to try and divide the ordered list of data values into 4 pieces of approximately equal length.

  1. Find the median
  2. Find by finding the median of the lower half of the data.
  3. Find , the median of the upper half of the data.
Example example
✎ Explanation (added)

Step by step for (, even). Median: halfway between the 4th and 5th values, . Lower half: , whose median is . Upper half: , whose median is . The three cut points split the list into four pieces with two values each. With an even the median is not a data value, so the halves are unambiguous.

Typed note included in the PDF Odd n: the median is a single data point

With an odd count, the median is one of the actual values, so you must decide whether it goes into the halves. There are two conventions, and they give different answers.

Example ():      (the 5th value)

Method A: exclude the median (TI-84, most intro courses)

Method B: include the median in both halves (Devore’s fourths)

Typed note included in the PDF Aran’s typed note (large, bold and underlined in the PDF)

Choose either methods when odd; Instructor will accept both answers.

When there is an odd number of data values, we need to determine what to do with the median (it will be a data value).

  1. Include it in the lower half, but not the upper half
  2. Include it in the upper half, but not the lower half
  3. Exclude from both the upper and lower halfs   ← Math 1160 book says do this (agrees with the TI calculators)
  4. Include it in both.   ← Our book says to do this.

✱ It doesn’t really matter

✎ Explanation (added)

Why it “doesn’t really matter”: quartiles are only meant to cut the data into four roughly equal parts, and with a realistic amount of data the different conventions give nearly the same cut points. With nine values the difference looks large (IQR 12.5 versus 8) only because the data set is tiny. On a test, say which convention you used. The examples on the board follow the book (option 4, include the median in both halves). The TI-84’s 1-Var Stats uses option 3, so its Q1 and Q3 can differ from the board’s when is odd.

Textbook · Devore — Devore’s rule for odd n, in the Definition on p. 40: the median is included in both halves. This is option (4) on the board.

4Outliers and the 1.5 × IQR rule

Outliers:

When drawing the box plot, we start by drawing the central rectangle from to .

Since we didn’t compute the mean or standard deviation, let’s use the middle of the central rectangle as an estimate for the mean and use the IQR as an estimate for the standard deviation. This is only used to help explain how to find outliers.

✎ Explanation (added)

This connects to the end of Lecture 2, where an outlier was a value more than 2 standard deviations from the mean. He copies that rule using only things a box plot has: the middle of the box plays the role of the mean and the width of the box (the IQR) plays the role of the standard deviation. So “2 standard deviations from the mean” becomes “2 IQRs from the middle of the box”.

Textbook · Devore — outliers: Definition in §1.4, p. 42. Devore also splits them: more than 1.5 fₛ from the nearest fourth is an outlier, and more than 3 fₛ is an extreme outlier (otherwise mild). Example 1.20 and Figure 1.21 (pp. 42–43) show both kinds.

5Drawing a box plot

Rule How to draw a box plot

[To draw a] box plot, start by drawing the central rectangle from to .

Then draw a line through the central rectangle at the median.

Draw the left wisker (or lower whisker) from to the smallest data value that is not an outlier.

Draw the right whisker (or upper whisker) from to the largest data value that is not an outlier.

Finally, draw an asterisk at the coordinate for each outlier and then title and label the box plot.

The first two words are above the top edge of the photo; “To draw a” is the natural completion.

Textbook · Devore — how to draw a boxplot: §1.4, pp. 40–41, Example 1.19 with Figures 1.19 and 1.20; boxplots that show outliers, pp. 42–43.

✎ Explanation (added)

“Inclusive or” means “one or the other or both”. The overlap is part of the union. In everyday speech “or” often means one but not both; in probability it never does unless that is said explicitly.

7Experiments, sample spaces, events and the probability axioms

Definition

We will think of an experiment as any process with more than one possible outcome, one of which must occur.

An event will be a set consisting of possible outcomes.

The sample space will be the set of all possible outcomes. We will usually denote the sample space with .

✎ Explanation (added)

This is why the set operations were reviewed first: an event is a set of outcomes, a subset of . So “ or happens” is the set , “both happen” is , and “ does not happen” is . The sample space plays the role of the universal set.

Textbook · Devore — sample space: Definition in §2.1, p. 53. Event (simple or compound): Definition on p. 54.

Example

Consider flipping a coin.

Let’s suppose there are two outcomes, we get heads or we get tails.

The sample space is   .

The event is said to have occurred if the result of the flip is heads.

The event is said to have occurred if the result of the flip is tails.

We expect both to happen with equal frequency.

We expect that 50% of the time we will get heads and will get tails 50% of the time.

We will say the probability we get heads is 50% or or 0.50.

We will say the probability of getting tails is 50% (or or 0.50).

We will write     and   .

↑ one of these must occur.

✎ Explanation (added)

Notation: takes an event (a set) and returns a number. is short for . The statement just says that something in the sample space is certain to happen, which is built into the definition of an experiment (“one of which must occur”).

Textbook · Devore — Example 2.1, p. 53, is the two-outcome experiment.

Theorem Probability assignments must satisfy the following
  1. For any ,   .
  2. .
  3. For any pairwise disjoint collection of events ,

Side note with an arrow to : book says this must hold for any countably infinite collection of sets and then shows that it means it is also true for a finite collection.

✎ Explanation (added)

In words: (1) a probability is never negative; (2) the whole sample space has probability 1; (3) if events cannot happen together, the probability that one of them happens is the sum of their probabilities. Pairwise disjoint means every pair has an empty intersection, ; another name is mutually exclusive. The coin obeys all three: , , and and are disjoint with . These are the axioms in Devore §2.2; everything else about probability is derived from them.

Textbook · Devore — the three axioms: §2.2, p. 58. Devore states Axiom 3 for an infinite collection of disjoint events and then shows it also holds for a finite collection, as the board’s side note says.

The empty [set] is denoted by writing or .

Why each step is allowed: , so the first equality changes nothing. The empty set is disjoint from itself (), so axiom 3 lets the probability of the union be split into a sum. That leaves a number equal to twice itself, , and the only such number is . This is the first example of deriving a property from the axioms.

Textbook · Devore — P(∅) = 0: Proposition in §2.2, p. 58, proved the same way. The null event and mutually exclusive (disjoint) events are defined on p. 56.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • A data set of about 9 to 15 numbers: find the five-number summary and the IQR, stating the convention you used for the quartiles if is odd.
  • Find the outlier fences and and list any outliers.
  • Draw the box plot: box, median line, whiskers to the last values that are not outliers, asterisks for outliers, a title and a labelled axis.
  • Two small sets and a universal set: list the elements of , , and , or shade them on a Venn diagram.
  • Write down the sample space for a simple experiment and state the three probability axioms.
  • Show from the axioms that .
